I love this SCP and I upvoted it instantly, but now I won't get off my head Voct's questions…I think that, without affecting the quality of this article, the author could update it with a few more tests -like one or two, especially the ones involving drawing. Moreover, what about laughter? Is it considered a phrase by the notepad or not? More generally: is EVERY sound produced by human vocal chords considered as a word/phrase or does 546 affect just proper words? If so, does one ever have lapsuses? Of course, as yoric said this SCP raises a [expletive]-ton of questions and this is what makes it beautiful…still the curiosity will make my liver twist and twitch 'till I won't think to it anymore.
Well done, generic author whose name is unknown to me!

To be honest, SCPs that involve language and meaning always make me think of this kind of question. At least the typo pope's effect is simple: you always make a mistake when describing it, no matter what language you use. And you can't accurately copy a phrase about the pupa in a language you don't know, because whoever wrote that sentence will have made a mistake.

The 'opposite pen', on the other hand, I loathe, because what exactly counts as an 'opposite' and which 'intent' is being used and so on.

I like to think there would be additional documents for most SCPs detailing all the varied experiments they performed on them. Extended Test Logs and all that. Assuming they even bothered to; I would think an SCP like this wouldn't warrant a lot of resources. I can't think of many useful uses for it, there are probably hundreds of different variations you could test (some Japanese characters have lots of pronunciations, illiterate people, etc.) and every test requires a D-class to be performed.

Mostly, I'm not sure if the article would be improved by adding a ton more tests.

item.title: Hm
item.content:encoded:
Here's a shitload of questions.

Do you have to know the meaning of what you wrote/transcribed? Is it enough to know the pronunciation?

What happens if you write a string of numbers? Or an equation? What happens if you draw something instead of write? If you draw a red octagon with the word STOP on it, do you say "STOP STOP STOP" or "STOP SIGN STOP SIGN STOP SIGN" ? What about "SMILEY FACE" , or "SIDEWAYS SMILEY FACE", or "ASTERISK"? Is "$100" pronounced "one hundred dollars" or "dollar sign hundred"?

Do you say "nine oh two one oh" or "nine zero two one zero" or "ninety thousand two hundred ten" or "ninety thousand two hundred and ten" ?

What if you write the word "POLISH"? Do you say it as in 'polish' or as in 'Polish'? Do you have access to both pronunciations?

What if you use mirror-writing?

What if you're given a string of random letters to transcribe? How would you pronounce "fbnmsdyyyfguhaskuyrnnnBfgylKWEF" , for instance?

What if you're given a string of non-English characters to copy, whose pronunciation you don't know? Cyrillic, for instance, or Hebrew or Greek or Armenian or (god help us) pinyin?

How long can you wait between writing components of a phrase before the paper 'decides' that the phrase is complete? If you wrote "South Dixie" and then waited ten minutes, and wrote "Driv", and then waited another ten minutes before adding the final 'e', would you be saying "South Dixie Drive", "South Dixie Driv", or just "South Dixie"?

What happens if you draw a map?

If you cut off a piece of this paper, do both pieces maintain the anomalous property?

What happens if you print a document on a piece of this paper? It says "any writing instrument", after all; that should include a laser printer. What happens if I print a document on the paper, but you're the one who wrote it?

What if you write musical notation? Do you have to sing everything from that point forward? What if you trace musical notation but you can't read music?

What if you're wearing muddy sneakers with an embossed logo on them, and you walk across a piece of this paper and the logo gets stamped on the paper in mud? What if the logo is smeared into illegibility?

We should probably have a lot more sheets of this, to be honest.

(More thoughts later.)

item.content:encoded: I like this, and upvoted it. One very minor thing I want to mention. The picture seems to imply the tests were done sequentially, with no other tests in between. Strictly speaking then, they really shouldn't be using different phrases in the third and fourth test. Controlling variables is very important when doing science-y things, and you shouldn't just randomly change the phrase unless you wanted to test what happens with a different phrase. It could be different phrases would produce different results (I don't know if sign language has a sign for '-', but if not it could be conceivable that's why that test didn't affect signing). Not saying I think the article would be improved by changing it; the picture would kind of be boring with the same phrase written out over and over. But the inner scientist in me just felt like posting this.

item.content:encoded:
SCP-546 is to be contained in a secured lock box.
…
At no point should SCP-546 or any of the sheets leave the quarantine room.

There's no mention of a quarantine room prior to the statement that the item isn't to leave it. Is the lock box in the quarantine room? Does it need to be taken there before being unlocked? Could do with a spot of clarification.

Besides the anomalous effects of the item, the SCP has no other outstanding characteristics.

This is saying, "Aside from what isn't normal, it's normal." You can cut this sentence and lose nothing.

The frequency of the phrase will continue to rise over the course of time.

This sentence is wonky, I'd revise it to something like, "The prevalence of the phrase increases over time." You could also combine this sentence and the one which follows.

unable to write and speak anything else other than

"Else" is entirely superfluous here.

Although there is serious mental distress from losing the ability to communicate with others, affected subjects have been shown to be able to continue living on with their new disability.

Could condense that to, "Aside from distress due to inability to communicate, affected subjects have displayed no further detrimental effects."

I'm indifferent toward this. Doesn't grab me at all.

"The subject was calmed down, and then asked to continue singing the song, except this time in English. This time, the phrase did not occur until after 2 hours have passed. A written test phase later did not produce the same anomaly."

The last sentence isn't clicking in my brain. What anomaly didn't occur? Maybe just me.

Either way, I think this SCP is excellent. It definitely passes the "knowledge this object is in your house makes you want to jump out the window" test. If I were affected by it, I'd be jumping off the nearest bridge.

There's part of me that really wants to dislike this because it has no real 'cool' factor - many many SCPs on the site are horrifying, but are still 'cool'; they'd be entertaining in a short story or movie. This isn't cool, just simple, ordinary, and awful. Upvoted.
